adults.title: Promises That Keep Reaching
adults.big_idea: The infinite power of God is in our covenants; it reaches across generations, and no one we love has wandered beyond it.
adults.objective: Learners will be able to explain from Elder Morgan's words and the scriptures how covenants bless more than the person who makes them, and will leave with renewed hope for someone they pray for.
prepare: Read Elder Jeremiah J. Morgan's talk, The Infinite Power of God in Our Covenants, and mark paragraphs 10–12 and 17–22.
Bring a small card or slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write on the board before class: What lies in my power? What is God's to do?
Ask two people ahead of time to be ready to read the key quotes from paragraphs 18 and 21 aloud.
Pray by name for the people in your class who are carrying worry for a loved one.

segments.name: Two names
steps: After the opening prayer, give each person a card. Explain that no one will be asked to show it.
Invite them to write silently the first name of one person who came before them whose faith has blessed their life, and one person they carry in their prayers.
Say that today's talk is about what God does between those two names. Ask them to keep the card in front of them.

segments.name: “It was covenants”
steps: Retell Elder Morgan's story briefly: each morning when he was a young teenager his mother read the Book of Mormon aloud to him. He remembers only two phrases from it, but he knew it mattered to her and that she knew it was true. He was raised in a different church that also believes in the Book of Mormon. At 14 he began to seek, attended both congregations for two months, and came to know this is the Lord's Church.

Explain that later, as he retold this experience, he wondered aloud why a young boy would care so much about religion. His wife, Rebecca, answered that it was covenants: his third-great-grandparents had made covenants in the temple in Nauvoo.
Have someone read the first key quote (paragraph 15).
Invite pairs to discuss the questions, then take two or three responses.
questions: Elder Morgan remembers almost none of the words his mother read, yet her effort changed him. When has someone's faithfulness reached you more than their words did?
What do you notice about who made the covenants that reached him?

segments.name: How far does a promise reach?
steps: Divide into two groups (or pairs taking one passage each).
Group one reads Doctrine and Covenants 2:2 with paragraphs 14–16 of the talk. Group two reads Enos 1:15–18 with paragraphs 17–18.
Ask each group to prepare one sentence that answers: What does this teach about how long and how far God's promises reach?
Have each group share its sentence and write it on the board. Ask the reader you assigned to read the key quote from paragraph 18.
Read aloud Elder Morgan's sentence in paragraph 14 about agency, and ask the question below.
questions: Elder Morgan teaches both that covenants do not alter the agency of children and that they have a discernible impact on posterity. How do those two truths fit together in your experience?

segments.name: For those who are waiting
steps: Say that Elder Morgan spoke directly to those who wonder whether they or a loved one have wandered too far. Read the words of President Holland that he quoted (aligned quote, paragraph 19).
In pairs, read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1 and then 123:17. Ask pairs to notice where the first verse begins and where the second arrives.
Have your second reader read the key quote from paragraph 21.
Point to the two questions on the board. As a class, list answers under each from paragraphs 21–22. Let the class do the listing.
Share Elder Rasband's words from this conference (aligned quote) and allow a moment of quiet.
questions: What lies in our power when someone we love is struggling? What have you learned to leave in God's hands?
What has helped you keep your covenants cheerfully while an answer is still coming?

segments.name: Say it in a sentence
steps: Ask each person to turn the card over and finish this sentence in writing: Because the power of God is in covenants, I can…
Invite three or four people to read their sentence. Listen for both truths: God's reach is without limit, and each person remains free to choose. Gently add whichever one is missing.

segments.name: Act and testify
steps: Elder Morgan gave no formal invitation, so invite each person to choose one of the actions listed under Act, or one the Spirit suggests, and write it on the card.
Read his promise to those who wait: “God hears you and will answer your prayers in His own time and in His own way.”
Bear your testimony of the Savior, whose Atonement Elder Morgan called the fulfillment of the greatest promise God made.
Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking what they noticed as they acted. Next week, ask: Where did you see the Lord's hand reaching toward your family?

key_quotes.text: It was covenants that had impacted me, not my covenants but the covenants of those who came before me. The power of God in those covenants reached out after me.
Like the great binding power of gravity that stretches across the universe, covenants with God stretch over all time and all space.
Take comfort; God hears you and will answer your prayers in His own time and in His own way.
Don’t ever give up. Your story, your family’s story, is not all written. God is the author and the finisher of it.

scriptures.use: Group one reads it with paragraphs 14–16 and looks for what the Lord plants in hearts and what turns as a result.
Group two reads it with paragraph 17 and looks for what Enos asked and what the Lord covenanted; then note Elder Morgan's point that this covenant took more than 2,000 years to be fulfilled.
Read in pairs as the honest cry of someone waiting on the Lord; Elder Morgan echoes it for parents of a struggling child.
Read in pairs right after 121:1; mark what we are to do and what we then wait to see God do, and use it to fill in the two questions on the board.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Jeffrey R. Holland
aligned_quotes.text: You have not traveled beyond the reach of divine love. It is not possible for you to sink lower than the infinite light of Christ’s Atonement shines.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Rasband
aligned_quotes.text: I ask you to turn over to Jesus Christ your despair for those wayward souls.

takeaways: The power of God in covenants does not stop with the person who makes them.
No one has wandered beyond the reach of God's love and the Savior's Atonement.
I can keep my covenants cheerfully and trust God with the rest of the story.
act: Pray each day by name for the person on your card, and end by telling Heavenly Father you trust His time and His way.
Read the Book of Mormon every day this week, aloud with someone if you can, even when it seems no one is listening.
Learn or retell the story of one person whose faithfulness came before yours, and share it with a family member.
Choose one covenant-keeping habit that lies in your power, such as partaking of the sacrament thoughtfully or worshipping in the house of the Lord, and do it cheerfully this week.
adapt: At home: skip the groups. Read Enos 1:15–18 and paragraphs 17–19 together, then let each person share one name they are praying for, if they wish.
Short on time: keep the two names, the story, and the waiting segment with Doctrine and Covenants 121:1 and 123:17.

Some in the class may be the first in their family to make covenants or may have no children. Point to Elder Morgan's words that we are all intended beneficiaries of countless covenants, and that covenants are generational in their impact.

youth.title: The Pull You Cannot See
youth.big_idea: The power of God in covenants reaches across generations to find us, and He leaves us free to answer.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain in their own words how covenants made by others can bless them, and will choose one thing to do this week with the testimony they already have.
prepare: Read Elder Jeremiah J. Morgan's talk, The Infinite Power of God in Our Covenants.
Bring a soft ball, paper, and pens. Ask youth to have scriptures or phones ready.
Write on the board: What is pulling on you that you cannot see?
Write the three honest questions from segment four on separate papers.

segments.name: Drop it
steps: As soon as class starts, ask everyone to hold a pen at arm's length and drop it on the count of three. Toss the ball up and catch it. Ask if anyone's pen floated.
Ask: You cannot see gravity. How do you know it is there? Does it ever skip a day?
Point to the question on the board and say that Elder Morgan compared something in the gospel to gravity. Their job is to work out what and why.

segments.name: Fourteen, behind the accordion doors
steps: Tell the story in about two minutes: Elder Morgan grew up in a different church that also believes in the Book of Mormon. His mother read the Book of Mormon aloud to him every morning before school, whether he was listening or not. He remembers only two phrases from it, but he knew she knew it was true.

Continue: at 14 he began to question and to seek sincerely. For two months he went to his family's congregation and also, secretly, to a congregation of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, hiding between the accordion doors of the overflow. He came to know this is the Lord's Church. It was some time before he could join, and he faced questions and disappointment from his family.
Ask partners to discuss the questions, then hear from a few.
questions: He knew some things and was confused about others at the same time. Where are you like that right now?
What would it take for you to seek an answer the way he did?

segments.name: Covenant hunt
steps: Explain that later Elder Morgan wondered why a boy his age cared about religion at all. His wife said, “It was covenants.” His third-great-grandparents had made covenants in the temple in Nauvoo.

Form two or three teams. Race: find Enos 1:15–18 and be the first team to say what Enos asked for and what the Lord covenanted. Then ask teams to guess how long that covenant took to be fulfilled. Give Elder Morgan's answer: more than 2,000 years.
Have every team read Doctrine and Covenants 2:2 and say what gets planted, and where.
Read the gravity key quote (paragraph 18). Each team writes a headline of eight words or fewer that captures it. Read the headlines aloud and let the class vote for the one they would remember.

segments.name: Three honest questions
steps: Lay out the three question papers. Let each trio pick one and prepare a 30-second answer using the paragraph listed.
Question one: Does my family's faith decide mine? (Paragraph 14: covenants do not alter agency, yet they have a discernible impact.)
Question two: What if I feel I have gone too far, or a friend has? (Paragraph 19, with President Holland's words. Add President Oaks's words from this conference, the aligned quote.)

Question three: What if I am the first in my family, or my family does not believe as I do? (Paragraph 18: we are all intended beneficiaries of countless covenants, and covenants bless more than the one who makes them. Elder Morgan himself faced questions and disappointment from his family when he came to know this is the Lord's Church.)
Hear each trio. Be honest that the pull is real and the choice is still theirs.

segments.name: What I know
steps: Have everyone read Joseph Smith—History 1:25 silently. Tell them Elder Morgan used Joseph's words to describe his own testimony at their age.
Give two minutes of silent writing on paper or in phone notes: one thing I know, and one thing I am still seeking.
Check for understanding: ask two volunteers to answer the board question in one sentence each. Listen for the covenants of others and God's love reaching toward them.

segments.name: This week
steps: Elder Morgan gave no formal invitation, so offer the challenges listed under Act and ask each person to choose one and tell a partner which.
Read the lesson Elder Morgan said he learned: “No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon.”
Read the key quote from paragraph 22 and bear a brief testimony that the Savior reaches for each of them.
Tell them you will start next week with a two-minute report. Next week, ask: What did you try, and what did you notice?

key_quotes.text: No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon.
Like the great binding power of gravity that stretches across the universe, covenants with God stretch over all time and all space.
Don’t ever give up. Your story, your family’s story, is not all written.

scriptures.use: Team race: find what Enos asked and what the Lord covenanted, then compare guesses with Elder Morgan's statement that it took more than 2,000 years to be fulfilled.
Teams read it and name what is planted in the hearts of the children; connect it to Elder Morgan's interest in religion at 14.
Read silently before the writing time; ask what Joseph was sure of even when others pushed back, and what each youth is sure of.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: He is relentless in His loving pursuit of each of you.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Patrick Kearon
aligned_quotes.text: He employs every possible measure to bring [us] back.

takeaways: God's power in covenants is real even when I cannot see it.
Covenants others have kept can bless me, and the choice to follow the Savior is still mine.
Neither I nor anyone I care about is beyond the reach of God's love.
act: Read the Book of Mormon every day for seven days, even for five minutes, and note one thing you feel rather than one thing you remember.
Ask a parent, grandparent, or leader to tell you about someone whose faith came before yours, and write down one detail.
Take the question you wrote under still seeking to Heavenly Father in prayer each day this week.
Send an encouraging message to a friend who feels far from God, without preaching; just let them know they matter.
music: As I Search the Holy Scriptures
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip the teams. Do the pen drop, tell the story, read Enos 1:15–18 together, and let each person choose one honest question to talk through.
Large class: give each question paper to several trios and hear one answer per question.
Short on time: keep the pen drop, the story, the gravity quote, and the weekly challenge.

children.title: Heavenly Father Keeps His Promises
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father always keeps His promises, and His love can reach me wherever I am.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Heavenly Father keeps His promises and will choose one way to listen to the Book of Mormon this week.
prepare: Read Elder Jeremiah J. Morgan's talk and be ready to tell the story of his mother in your own simple words.
Bring a soft ball, a flashlight, a copy of the Book of Mormon, paper, and crayons.
Practice the one sentence the children will repeat: Heavenly Father keeps His promises.
Clear a little space so children can stand, step, and move safely.

segments.name: Sing and gather
steps: Sing “Book of Mormon Stories” with simple actions, or march in place to the beat.
Invite a child to pray. Whisper together, then say in a regular voice: Heavenly Father keeps His promises.

segments.name: The ball always comes down
steps: Hold up the ball. Ask the children to guess what will happen when you let go. Drop it. Let several children take a turn dropping it.
Ask: Did it ever stay up? Explain that something we cannot see, called gravity, pulls the ball down every single time, everywhere.
Explain that a covenant is a special promise with Heavenly Father. Elder Morgan taught that God's power in covenants is like gravity: it reaches everywhere and never stops.
Have the children stretch their arms as wide as they can and say together: Heavenly Father keeps His promises.
questions: What is a promise? How do you feel when someone keeps a promise to you?

segments.name: A mother who read every day
steps: Tell the story: When Elder Morgan was a boy getting ready for school, his mother read the Book of Mormon out loud to him every day, whether he was listening or not, until it was finished.
Act it out. Choose one child to hold the Book of Mormon as the reader. The others pretend to get ready for school: brush teeth, comb hair, put on shoes, pick up a backpack. Switch readers and repeat.
Explain that he did not remember many of the words, but he knew the Book of Mormon was important to his mother and that she knew it was true. Later he knew it was true too.
Share his words: “No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon.”
questions: How do you think he could tell that his mother loved the Book of Mormon?

segments.name: A very long promise
steps: Hold up the Book of Mormon and tell the children that a man named Enos prayed for people who would live long after him. The Lord made a covenant with Enos that those people would someday receive the gospel of Jesus Christ.
Have the children take slow giant steps across the room while you say: a long time… a long, long time… more than two thousand years. At the other side, say together: And He kept His promise.
Walk back the same way and repeat once more.
questions: Does Heavenly Father forget His promises when a long time goes by?

segments.name: His love reaches me
steps: Turn on the flashlight and point it at the floor or a wall, never at eyes. Ask a child to stand near the light, then another to stand far across the room. Move the light to shine on the floor at each child's feet.
Ask: Could the light reach near? Could it reach far? Explain that Elder Morgan taught that no one is too far away for God's love to reach.
Share Elder Fale's words from this conference (the aligned quote) and say them together.
Give each child paper and crayons. Invite them to draw themselves in a place they like to be, with a bright light shining on them to show God's love reaching them there.

segments.name: My turn to listen
steps: Let two or three children show their drawing and say where God's love reaches them.
Check for understanding: ask, Who keeps His promises? and What book did the mother read every day? Let everyone answer together.
Invite each child to choose one way to listen to or read the Book of Mormon this week and tell it to the child beside them.
Sing “My Heavenly Father Loves Me” and share a short testimony that Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ love each child.
Next week, begin by asking: Who listened to the Book of Mormon this week? What did you hear?

key_quotes.text: No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon.
covenants with God stretch over all time and all space.

scriptures.use: Hold up the Book of Mormon while you tell about the Lord's covenant with Enos; an older child can read the verse aloud before the giant steps.
After the acting, tell the children the Lord asks us to remember the Book of Mormon, just as the mother in the story did; an older child can find and read the first part of the verse.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: God's love can reach me wherever I am.
Reading the Book of Mormon is never wasted.
act: Listen to or read the Book of Mormon every day this week, even a few verses.
Hang your drawing where you will see it and say: God's love can reach me.
Make one small promise to someone at home, such as putting away your shoes, and keep it.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep each part short and repeat the sentence Heavenly Father keeps His promises after every activity, with arms stretched wide. Let every child drop the ball and be the reader for a moment. Skip the questions that need long answers and add another round of giant steps. A helper can sit with children who need a hand with drawing.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Enos 1:16 aloud and another read the first part of Doctrine and Covenants 84:57. Ask a harder question: Why might Heavenly Father keep a promise even when it takes a very long time? Let an older child lead the giant steps or hold the flashlight, and invite them to write one sentence under their drawing about how God's love reaches them.
